Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON (continued)

Dr Bohin, welcome back from yesterday. We had just started to deal with your opinion relating to events on the four separate occasions and you had dealt at least in part with your opinion concerning [Baby I]'s first collapse on 30 September. But because that was foreshortened by the break, I'd just like to retread that ground if we may, if you'll forgive me for that.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Going back to your paragraph 5.12.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: You told us yesterday or had given us a summary of the circumstances which you had taken into account in reaching your opinion and I'd like you now, if you would, please, to give us your opinion for the events related to [Baby I]'s collapse at 16.30 and 19.30 on 30 September, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. In my opinion, the collapse of [Baby I] at that time was caused by administration of air into the nasogastric tube, via the nasogastric tube into the bowel.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Whilst you have explained the mechanism to us before as to why that would compromise a child like [Baby I], in short form perhaps, could you just remind us of the mechanism?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, of course. An excess amount of air within the bowel will cause the abdomen to distend, so become much fatter, and in turn, as well as becoming fatter, it pushes up on the diaphragm, the muscle between the chest and the abdomen, and that in turn squashes the lungs and affects respiration. We know that the lungs were not entirely normal in any case, so actually by squashing them that further compromises them and it in turn -that will then eventually cause a collapse.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So far as other possibilities were concerned, we've heard that there was a real-time caution about the possibility of NEC. Given all the circumstances, have you discounted that as being the cause of [Baby I]'s collapse on the 30th?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Necrotising enterocolitis has to be considered in any baby with a distended abdomen, but a distended abdomen is not the only feature of necrotising enterocolitis and [Baby I] had no other features of necrotising enterocolitis, either clinically or on X-ray, in my opinion.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So moving to 13 October next, please. Just to contextualise that event, it happened at about 03.20 that morning. It's the event when [Baby I] was in nursery 2 and the other nurse or the nurse who gave direct evidence about the circumstances was Ashleigh Hudson. Can you tell us what was, in your view, the cause of [Baby I]'s collapse on that occasion?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Again, in my opinion the appearances of the X-ray associated with the collapse and the discolouration of the abdomen can be accounted for by exogenous administration, so outside administration, of air via the nasogastric tube into the bowel and also an air embolus, ie air being deliberately administered into an intravenous line.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did you take into account particularly the appearances on the X-ray that I think we looked at yesterday at 4.25 on 13 October?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I did. There's no evidence of necrotising enterocolitis, there's no evidence of an obstruction and I couldn't find any pathological reason for the abdomen to have those appearances on X-ray.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Did you look specifically -- and I'm looking particularly at your paragraphs 5.11 and 5.12, did you look at the records to see whether there was -- whether you could establish the issue -- the presence or otherwise of an NGT being in place at the time?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think that's a really important point because historically, looking at all of these cases, the nursing staff were not particularly good at recording when they inserted or removed or change nasogastric tubes, despite their paperwork having boxes for nurses to fill that in.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It was often incomplete. So it's difficult looking at the notes to establish whether there was or was not a nasogastric tube in place.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: [Baby I] was bottle feeding and had been for several days so there was no clinical need for her to have a nasogastric tube in place. However, it is normal practice to leave a nasogastric tube in place for some days after a baby gets to full bottle feeds, just because it's an unpleasant procedure to undertake, and so you don't -- if a baby goes on to full bottle feeds, they
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: may be okay for a couple of days and then require tube feeds again.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So the nursing staff tend to leave them in for several days. I don't know what the policy is in Chester and there is no evidence that a tube was removed, but there was no evidence that a tube was replaced either.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: As a matter of practicalities, how long does it take to put in place an NGT?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: A matter of seconds.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And to remove it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Seconds.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What would the reasons why on this occasion you believe that air in the vein was a possibility?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The staff give a description of a bruiselike discolouration over the right side of the sternum and the medical staff made a comment that they thought this was down to the result of earlier chest compressions, so CPR. In my experience, CPR does not cause that sort of bruising.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Over the years, sadly, I've attended many, many resuscitations of newborn babies, both on a neonatal unit and in a regional cardiac unit, where CPR is much more common, but I have not seen children or babies end up with significant bruising over their chest to account for it, so I couldn't account for this discolouration from a pathological process and therefore I deduce from that that this was down to an air embolus associated with the ensuing collapse.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Moving on to events on 14 October, please, so this is number 3. We have two events fairly close in time, 00.55 and 07.00 or thereabouts, or 07.30, that sort of time. So it was the succeeding night shift, in other words.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What conclusions did you -- what was your opinion as to the reasons for [Baby I]'s collapse at that time?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Again, in my opinion, based on the appearances of the Xray, the discolouration of the abdomen and the collapse can be accounted for by the exogenous administration of air into the bowel and air embolus, ie air being inserted into a vein. My reasons for that were that as well as the bruising on the right side of the chest that was noted previously, the abdomen had become distended, hard and the staff noted spreading areas of
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: discolouration over the abdomen and then resuscitation was required within the hour.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The X-ray after that showed that there was widespread gaseous distension that we'd seen previously and I could find no clinical pathological reason for that appearance.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Moving on, finally, to the fourth occasion which we have examined in detail [Baby I]'s progress. We begin a couple of minutes before midnight of the 22nd into 23 October and then with [Baby I]'s final collapse and death, which was described to us yesterday by Dr Gibbs. What conclusions have you reached so far as the cause of [Baby I]'s death?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In my view, the cause of [Baby I]'s death was air embolus, that is air being injected into an intravenous line.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Are there any specific features of the evidence which in your opinion account for that as the cause?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: As well as the sudden and unexpected catastrophic collapse, the thing that was compelling to me was the issue of being unsettled and agitated and crying in a way that nurses felt was unusual. Babies cry for all sorts of reasons and parents and experienced nurses get a sense of why babies are crying, whether it's through hunger or brief discomfort, for example if a blood test is taken. But in those instances, babies can usually be consoled, so either by a cuddle -- not in this case, but either by a cuddle or some containment holding or some sucrose or a dummy. This was very different and the staff have said very clearly that this was different and this was inconsolable crying, which is extremely unusual in a baby and I think [Baby I] was in pain at this time and must have been in severe pain to be this upset and agitated.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: This, and the distension of the abdomen and the sudden collapse, led me to think that this was an air embolus.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Looking at it from the other end of the telescope, so to speak, in your view was there anything to support the suggestion that this collapse and death was the result of a normal "innocent" process?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Obviously I've considered a number of innocent processes, but I can think of nothing that would cause the mottling of the trunk. Dr Gibbs described that [Baby I] had a pink face, but her trunk and limbs were mottled, associated with her becoming very, very unsettled. That, to me, is a baby in pain and it may well have been that she was hypoxic at that point, ie there was low oxygen in her blood because that causes you to become agitated.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It doesn't cause you to have inconsolable crying, but hypoxia can cause you to be agitated.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The inconsolable crying is a baby in pain and that may be due to the fact that the heart has become starved of oxygen in the process of an air embolus. When air goes into the heart it can cause a lock in the heart, which effectively causes the collapse, which is what I think happened here, but that can be a painful process.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Would you remain there, please, Dr Bohin?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: There will be some further questions for you.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
In the case of every child in this trial, Dr Bohin, you received and read Dr Evans' opinions before providing an opinion of your own, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I was asked to peer-review Dr Evans' notes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We've heard about peer review. If we want your independent views of what may have happened, the way to do that would have been to give you the material without Dr Evans' reports and see what you concluded independently of Dr Evans, wouldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: My reports are independent views.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We don't know and we will never know what conclusions you would have drawn had you not been provided with Dr Evans' reports first.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct, but I have been appointed as an expert witness in this court and my duty is to give an independent view and that's what I've done.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you agree that as a basic principle of scientific method, if you want to get an independent assessment of a situation you have an experiment or a review conducted independently of the first one to compare?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm sorry, you've lost me. Could you repeat the question?
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you agree that as a simple part of scientific method, if you want to review or check one set of findings, you conduct an independent experiment elsewhere?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: That means doing it without working off the findings of the first one, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If I'm not mistaken, I think you're suggesting that I've merely rubber-stamped Dr Evans' reports, which I think is less than discourteous. What I've done is review these cases. I was asked by Cheshire Police to establish whether, having reviewed the cases, I agreed with Dr Evans, whether I disagreed with Dr Evans or whether I found a different cause. That is what I have done and already in the cases that we have heard there have been times when I have disagreed with Dr Evans' findings and also when I have introduced my own findings into my report. So this was not a rubber-stamping exercise.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: First of all, Dr Bohin, I have been nothing other than courteous to you throughout --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: This isn't going to be very helpful, Mr Myers. Let's just detach ourselves for a moment and concentrate on you putting questions and the witness answering those questions.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That is what I've been trying to do throughout, my Lord. Comments are being made about my questions both by this witness and the last one.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: If I may say so, the implication behind the questions was quite clear and that is what the witness picked up.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Very well, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: But let's just press on with the questions you want to ask.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The next thing, Dr Bohin, is I'm not suggesting you are rubber-stamping what Dr Evans says, but you are supporting what he has said so far as you feel able to do so.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Let me be clear that you don't misunderstand my question. What I mean is you are backing up what he has said so far as you feel able to do so.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I'm not backing up what he said: I'm reviewing the case and coming to my own opinions. And if that is in alignment with Dr Evans' view, then it's in alignment with Dr Evans' view, but on occasion it is not in alignment with Dr Evans' view.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And I suggest you would never have come up with air embolus in the way you are doing had you not first been exposed to Dr Evans' theories at the very least on air embolus.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I disagree.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Do you have a coherent theory of exactly how an air embolus presents?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: An air embolus can present in a variety of ways in neonates. It occurs very rarely. I happen to have seen it twice in my career. Once in a baby who was receiving ECMO therapy, which is a specific sort of therapy, on a cardiac unit, where babies are put on a kind of bypass machine as a temporary measure until their lungs or lungs and heart recover from their underlying illness.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And during that, unfortunately it's a known risk that you can get air embolus in that circuit and you can actually see that because you can see blood in the circuit because it is outside of the body, so babies are put on a heart lung bypass machine. I saw a patient who developed -- you could see bubbles in that and the child immediately had a cardiac arrest.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So that child was on ECMO, clearly was seriously ill, not the same as the cases that we've seen here, but for the other symptoms I can only go on what was reported in the literature and that presents either as a full, unexpected collapse and the person dies or it can present with a collapse where, after resuscitation, the person recovers.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Most of the studies, as we've already discussed in the trial, have been done in older children and adults.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: There may be a drop in blood pressure, there may be a drop in heart rate, there may be skin changes. The clinical presentation is wide and varied. So that is my theory on how air embolus presents.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The pathophysiology behind it is that if you inject air into an vein, normally that air will go to the right side of the heart and would be, if it was a small amount, just be absorbed and would not cause any problem at all. If it was a large amount, it may well cause a problem and may cause a collapse.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: This is not what we're talking about here because those -- in those instances there would be no skin changes or other
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: manifestations. The mechanism I am proposing is that air is injected into a vein, it goes into the right side of the heart and then goes across a small hole between the top two chambers of the heart called the foramen ovale. That is present in newborn babies and closes but it also remains patent in a large percentage of the population.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If that happens, then blood can go across that little hole and if you inject air, air can also go across that little hole. With pumping of the heart, it means air is then pumped round the left side -- through the left side of the heart and around the circulation and can lodge in the skin and other organs.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Additionally, the volume of air may be such that it's so large that -- well, large, but we're talking -- in a baby it's a small volume of air but large enough to fill the chamber of the heart, in which case the heart stops.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Additionally, if air goes across the PFO, the small hole between the right and left upper chambers, and is pumped around the body, it will also get pumped into the coronary arteries, which are arteries that actually supply the heart with oxygen. So in adults you know that when people have a heart attack, their coronary arteries get blocked. The coronary arteries receive their oxygen. Once the left side of the heart pumps the blood goers round the body but also supplies the heart muscle itself with oxygen and in this case, I think as well as air being distributed round the body, it is likely, certainly theoretically likely, that air went down the coronary arteries.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What you say about discolouration and air embolus changes from case to case, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't think so.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What you say about the likelihood of collapse and not being able to resuscitate changes from case to case, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What you say about distress appears in some cases, doesn't appear in other cases, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: With any clinical condition, there are a number of clinical features that one might see, but you don't need to have all of those features to make the diagnosis. So you don't have to have distress in every single case, you don't have to have skin lesions in every single case. As we've discussed before, skin lesions don't appear in the literature in every single case.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What you are doing, I suggest, Dr Bohin, is you're adapting the allegation of air embolus to cover any situation in this case where you don't find any other cause to identify and blame the collapse upon.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, that's not the case. What I have done is look for pathological -- plausible pathological causes for the collapse. I didn't find one.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes, and what you're doing when you don't find one, when you say you don't find one, is just reaching for air embolus as a general catch-all and simply trying to attach whatever the clinical findings are to it.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, that's not the case.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Let me just pause and look at what you say about discolouration and event 4. We'll come to event 4 in due course, but whilst I'm asking this question.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There's nothing in event 4, the 22nd into 23 October, that marks out any discolouration indicative of air embolus, is there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Which part of my report are you referring to?
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Well, I'm asking you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Give me a moment, I'll find it.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: (Pause)
Dr Gibbs was struck by purple-white discolouration of the skin.
Dr Gibbs gave evidence yesterday, didn't he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You heard that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: He described mottling.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Which is not remarkable, is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not necessarily, no.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: He described the colouring on both occasions as due to poor perfusion, didn't he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: He said it may be a sign of poor perfusion, but he also said that the face was white and the trunk and limbs were mottled and he was struck by that difference.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: He said that, dealing with the first part of this, there was a problem with the circulation. That's what he believed. It's in his evidence yesterday.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, there was because she'd collapsed.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: He expected that that would improve with saline; do you remember him saying that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And he said it did over the next few minutes when she was given saline.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: He's described something that's quite unremarkable in colouring with poor circulation, dealt with by saline, hasn't he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: On that particular occasion, but when he was called back there was purple-white discolouration of the skin again.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Let's deal with that one first of all because you have relied on that to tell this jury that's supporting evidence of air embolus, haven't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In fact, if that's an air embolus, it's not going to be dealt with by a saline infusion, is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: A saline infusion will improve the circulation. So with air embolus, depending on the volume of air that's been administered, you will either collapse and die and there will be no amount of resuscitation that can save you, or you may survive with active resuscitation, and in this case, on the first event, [Baby I] survived with active resuscitation, including a bolus of saline.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And Dr Gibbs regarded nothing out of the ordinary for the circumstances of poor circulation with that colouring, did he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't remember him saying that it was nothing out of the ordinary.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: He's not described anything out of the ordinary, has he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, he described the mottling, which is not normal.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Mottling is very normal for [Baby I], Dr Bohin.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If it was very normal, people wouldn't have commented on it. Where things were normal for [Baby I], like a distended abdomen, people quite often said in their notes, "Normal for [Baby I]", but then went on to say, when her abdomen became bigger, this was out of the ordinary.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So I think if [Baby I] was mottled all the time, people would not have mentioned it. This must have been out of the ordinary for them to have mentioned it.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Are you saying there's no other references to [Baby I] being mottled in the notes?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I'm not saying that. I'm saying she may well have been mottled but for people to have written this down at the time of her collapse, it must have been out of the ordinary.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Mottled is written down in many places of the notes of [Baby I], isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Not because it's out of the ordinary, it's just how she presented.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. It may have been but she didn't present always mottled with a collapse.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And the second part of that incident, again Dr Gibbs described that as being what appeared to him to be poor perfusion, didn't he?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, she'd collapsed, so yes, he wasn't thinking of air embolus.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And there's absolutely nothing specific about that discolouration that makes that characteristic of an air embolus, Dr Bohin, is there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, discolouration is not pathognomonic of air embolus but is consistent with air embolus.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And this case, so far as has been dealt with up to now, if I understand it correctly, is the issue of discolouration with air embolus is that it's quite a specific discolouration --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, it isn't.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Right. So you no longer maintain that what's described in, for example, the article by Lee and Tanswell is a characteristic description?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I do, but if you ask anyone to look at a description of a rash, you will get very different answers about the same type of rash. So I'm reliant on people writing what they see in a cardiac arrest situation where they've got lots of other things to write. So we're unlikely to get a huge amount of detail about the rash because they've got so much else to be considering.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So I think that in air embolus, the type of rash -- you may get linear lines, you may get the circular lesions. There are a number of things you may get with air embolus and I think the staff have described that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So there could be any number of discolourations now which are air embolus, is that where we are?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: [Baby I] was poorly on many occasions from her birth, wasn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: She's extremely preterm at 27 weeks, wasn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And extremely low birth weight?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And throughout the notes you've seen, there are problems that are consistent and recur, aren't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And that includes desaturation, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It includes abdominal distension on a variety of occasions, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it does.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And actually, mottling is described in her notes on a number of occasions, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

So with infection or abdominal distension, if feeds are stopped and you've got no calorie intake you are not going to put on weight appropriately during that time. That is part and parcel of being a premature neonate: nutrition is paid attention to but the other aspects of care are much more important initially than nutrition.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Additionally, when [Baby I] was fed, she was fed breast milk, which is absolutely the right thing for premature babies. blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, no idea at all, and I don't think anybody has any idea. I can find no research papers. It's so variable -- it would be so variable depending on the size of the baby, whether the baby had been fed.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: A stomach that has never had any milk in it will be quite small. You need to remember that the stomach is a muscle so it can stretch.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But it's a bit like a balloon the first time -- babies, when they're born, their stomach is very small and you give them a little bit of milk the first day and a bit more the next day and a bit more the next day in normal term babies and so their stomach stretches.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, the plan was to transfer out on the 15th because this was a level 2 unit who don't routinely deal with long-term ventilated patients and she had had a cardiac arrest for which the team did not have an obvious cause.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So they were in liaison with a tertiary centre and, just before 4 o'clock on 15 October, there was another deterioration, which required re-intubation. But she was always going to be transferred out because it was their policy not to keep ventilated patients long-term.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Could we look at the radiograph, please, on pages 14701 and 14702? This is a radiograph taken on 15 October 2015 at 15.31.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can we scroll down to what Dr Wright, who's the radiologist, said about this? This is 15.30 on the 15th. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It describes the position of the ET tube and the NG tube. There's nothing I'm drawing out from the top part of that, it's what's in the second part that I'd like us to go to:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Right-sided long line in situ with its tip projected over the inferior vena cava at L1 level."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: "There's been a marked interval change in the bowel gas pattern. No free intraperitoneal air noted. The bowel is centrally located with peripheral opacification compatible with ascites. Bowel wall oedema is also noted."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Ascites is fluid in the peritoneum, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: As it happens, that can be an early sign of NEC, can't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I have not seen ascites on an X-ray like that with NEC, no.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Ascites may indicate an inflammatory process ongoing?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It might, but actually she didn't have ascites.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But there may have been an inflammatory process ongoing?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't think there was.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Bowel wall oedema is also noted."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Is that liquid or fluid in the bowel wall or swelling because of --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That means actual thickening of the intestinal wall.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: With fluid?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Which again is consistent with an inflammatory process potentially, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It may be, but of course the report on the X-ray needs to be taken in conjunction with the clinical findings.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So the clinicians will obviously take note of that and the fact that one lung was collapsed and the other lung was hyperinflated. But the bowel is decompressed because she's got a nasogastric tube in place, and yes, that X-ray does show that there may be ascites. It's compatible with ascites. It doesn't mean that she's got ascites. If that doesn't fit with the clinical picture, which it doesn't, then she didn't have ascites and didn't have ascites.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: She had deteriorated dramatically over a period of days, hadn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She had had two events previously and had another deterioration that day, which led to her being re-intubated.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Can I ask you to clarify something, please? Did [Baby I] have a collapsed left lung at the time she was transferred to Arrowe Park Hospital?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, she was re-intubated.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Can I just ask you to explain something in your report at paragraph 5.21? You're referring to events on 15 October and the re-intubation then, aren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And you say something -- you say:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "It was appropriate to re-intubate [Baby I] at the time. The collapse of the left lung is most likely to be due to the ET tube being too long [and you put] +/- infection."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What does that mean?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, earlier [Baby I] had collapsed and -- well, she'd had a deterioration and at the time the team weren't sure why she had deteriorated. So it was completely appropriate to think that it might be an endotracheal tube-related issue so they took the old tube out and replaced it.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The X-ray after that replacement was that X-ray that you have just shown, which showed that one lung was white and was opacified, so that lung was collapsed.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The other lung looked like it was slightly larger than usual, which means that the endotracheal tube is preferentially ventilating one lung rather than two lungs, and that was why I said that the collapse of the left lung was most likely due to the endotracheal tube being too long.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: What does "+/- infection" mean?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There may be infection to play -- there may be infection as well to play in that. At that stage it wasn't known, but there may be and she was screened for infection.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I'm going to move to the 22nd into 23 October 2015, which is event 4 or events 4. I'd just like to be clear about what you say is or may be the cause of this or these events. I'm looking at the final page of your report.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In your evidence this morning, Dr Bohin, you have said that this collapse or these collapses are due to air embolus, haven't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I want to understand. In the report that you wrote, you put:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I agree with Dr Evans that the collapse on 22/23 October is likely to be secondary to an air embolus, but I also think [or 'say'] that there was exogenous administration of air into the bowel via the NGT and that neither of these was accidental."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just so we know, in terms of your evidence now, what's happened to the suspicion that this was due to air down the NGT, which is what you said in your report?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I still think that's a possibility.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: On the basis of the radiograph at 00.23?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So your evidence in fact is that this is air down the NGT and air embolus?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And is that on event 1 of event 4 or event 2 or events 1 and 2?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Both.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So on both occasions you're saying there has been someone deliberately putting air intravenously and into the NGT?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I can't be clear of which one of those -- whether both of them occurred on both events or one occurred on each of the events. But the way that [Baby I] presented is compatible with both air embolus and exogenous air down the nasogastric tube.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: You've heard the evidence of Nurse Hudson, haven't you, about how she checked the abdomen when [Baby I] first collapsed?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And she identified no sign of distension or swelling?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I want to ask you about what you say about air embolus here. When you were giving evidence about this, you said it's air embolus because the event was sudden and unexpected, [Baby I] had been unsettled and agitated. She was in, you said, severe pain, there was distension of the abdomen and collapse, and there was mottling.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's what you said, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Can you help us with how distension of the abdomen is supportive of air embolus?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Distension of the abdomen is not supportive of air embolus but it is supportive of exogenous air down the nasogastric tube.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: It also follows a period after which air had been administered to [Baby I] as part of the support she was given, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But she had a nasogastric tube in place, which should decompress the bowel and would not cause that extent of bowel dilatation.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I'm not going to go back to Nurse Hudson's evidence, I've asked you about that. I'll stay with the other points I'm asking about air embolus.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Crying and distress, Dr Bohin, are highly subjective to gauge, aren't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We've heard the evidence of Nurse Hudson. Whatever the reason for that, it is very speculative, isn't it, to jump from that to saying that must be because of an air embolus?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: What was described was something over and above normal crying in a baby. Nurse Hudson gave a very clear description of inconsolable crying and, for me, that is very unusual in a baby and indicates that they are in significant pain. There aren't many things that will cause that, but air embolus is one and, along with the other clinical findings here, it's compatible with air embolus and I think it was air embolus.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Well, I take issue with you on that, but I'm not going to repeat the questions.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As to the nature of the collapse, [Baby I] made an extremely good recovery very rapidly from the first deterioration, didn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Which is not consistent with the effect of an air embolus, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It can be because it depends on how much air has been injected.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And as for discolouration, I dealt with that when we began the questioning and I'm not going to repeat that now (inaudible: coughing) the points are that we make, Dr Bohin.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's entirely possible, isn't it, that for a baby who had been as poorly as [Baby I] had been, the cumulative effect of successive episodes meant that she was far more likely to deteriorate, sadly, and die in the way she did on 23 October, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I don't agree with that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And a baby who has undergone successive incidents like that will be weaker and less able to cope with the impact of a collapse and more likely, sadly, to die, and that's the fact of it, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, it's not, I'm afraid. She recovered from that first event and was so well that she was extubated. That didn't show a child that was in any way weakened or compromised.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Illness in neonates is -- there is no cumulative effect which means that there is then a tipping point, and you can't cope anymore. It doesn't work like that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The fact is that she was successfully resuscitated after that first event and that didn't in any way weaken her, meaning that with the next event she was more likely to succumb, so I'm afraid I can't agree with that.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I suggest you, in fact, cannot with any certainty identify any particular mechanism for how she came to die.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I think she had an air embolus.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And that is something that I suggest you have put together out of available pieces of evidence, Dr Bohin.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's not the case.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Re-examination by MR JOHNSON
Just a couple of issues, please, doctor.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Towards the beginning of the questions that you were asked on behalf of Lucy Letby, you were asked about two separate occasions on the 5th and 6 September --
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- if you remember that.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: As a matter of fact, it's right, isn't it, that those were dealt with in your report from paragraph 4.12 onwards?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And why didn't you flag those up as being incidents of concern?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Because she had an infection, she had clinical signs of an infection, she had a high white cell count, a high neutrophil
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: count, which is compatible and indicative of a bacterial infection, and a high platelet count of 906, which you see where there is a lot of inflammation.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And so by comparing those to the incidents that we've focused on here, in other words 30 September, 13 October, 14 October and the 22nd into 23 October, is that comparing like with like?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, I felt that [Baby I] had an infection at this point and also the X-ray taken around that time showed gas within the centre of the abdomen, which we have seen, but there was no evidence of NEC and there wasn't huge gaseous dilatation. So infection was the cause of that deterioration, so it wasn't a suspicious event to me, so there was no need to flag it as one.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But the lead-up to those events and the recovery from those events, were they typical of infective events?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. She continued to be unwell for a while and required intubation. She then became unwell whilst on the ventilator. So as I mentioned, she was known to have an infection, she was being treated for an infection, and had a very rocky time for a few days until the antibiotics controlled the infection and then she recovered.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And are they characteristics that we see with any of the four events that you have told us about in your evidence before cross-examination?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No. In the other events, she's collapsed and been resuscitated and either recovered very quickly or, sadly, on the last event was unable to be resuscitated.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: This event, where she had an infection, presented very differently and she recovered very differently.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Is that the very reason why you have highlighted the four events that you have as being suspicious?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, because they stood out.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Secondly, the nasogastric tube point. I'm referring here to the questions that you were asked about your analysis, such as you were able to analyse the notes, concerning whether or not [Baby I] had a nasogastric tube on 13 October; all right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: The issue being, if she didn't, how did the air get into her stomach? And I think you told us, when I was asking you
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: questions, that it is a matter of seconds for someone who knows how to do it to get a nasogastric tube into the stomach of a small baby.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And it can be removed equally quickly?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: As a matter of fact, at page 25 of your report, and it's paragraph 5.33, this also deals with the point that was suggested to you that you are a mere cipher for Dr Evans, did you confront the apparent -- the issue -- it's the third or fourth bullet point --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- did you confront this issue and summarise your position?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. I stated --
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Can you tell the jury what you said, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "I disagree in part with Dr Evans about the cause of the collapse on 13 October. As no nasogastric tube was present prior to the collapse, the amount of gas within the abdomen could be secondary to resuscitative bagging via face mask prior to intubation. Having said that, the appearances are gross and in excess of what I would expect to see after a period of bagging. I would agree with Dr Evans that exogenous administration of air into the bowel via the nasogastric tube is, on the balance of probabilities, the most likely cause."
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes, thank you. So is what you are saying there that there's no evidence on the face of the records to say that there was a tube in place?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: But getting the air in via that means is the one you favoured as a matter of opinion?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Can I deal finally with the weight issue that was raised with you. Can I ask Mr Murphy to put up on the screens pages 15029 and 15030 in the medical records.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I don't know if we can put them side by side, the two pages, if that's possible, or one above the other.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: All right. Sorry. As usual, I didn't give Mr Murphy any advance warning of what I'd ask him to do.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: This actually is a simple plot of [Baby I]'s weight, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: We can see along the west/east axis at the top of the graph "day 1" and the date above it; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So day 1 is 7 August and this runs to day 53, which is 28 September?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Here we have a fairly linear progression of [Baby I]'s weight. If we go on to the next page, please, Mr Murphy. Obviously, that one runs into the second one.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So it's taken up at the point the first one left off and we can see the continuation of that weight gain. Most markedly we see between about the 13th/14th -- it's actually from 10 October onwards, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: There's quite an increase. Did that, as a matter of fact, coincide with [Baby I] first being removed from the Countess of Chester and then subsequently returning?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, partly that time. It covers that time. She wasn't actually at the Countess of Chester.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Now, of course the point you've accepted is one has to look at the centiles; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So it's not simple a matter of looking at this graph and saying that she's gaining weight so that's all fine, because you would hope that if a child remains on the same centile, she would gain weight more quickly; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, but premature babies invariably cross centile lines at the start, so when she was born, she was on the 50th centile at 27 weeks' gestation. All babies lose a bit of weight, but premature babies will often cross centile lines before they settle on a line and grow along that centile line. So it was no surprise that she dropped from the 50th centile, but thereafter she didn't grow appropriately but she's been ill. This graph shows that actually she did gain weight, so her weight wasn't completely static.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. Is that really a graphic, literally in a graph, representation of the point you were making before?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. Does your Lordship have any questions?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I don't, thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Bohin. That completes your evidence in relation to this part of the case, but you'll be coming back to give further evidence. So please don't talk to anyone about anything to do with the case.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

Summary of interview with LUCY LETBY re [Baby I]
(read)
The usual warning applies to this, ladies and gentlemen. It's a very short summary of some very long interviews.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: On 4 July 2018, the interviewing officers followed the relevant medical notes from the outset. Of the first incident, on 30 September 2015, Lucy Letby had no independent recollection and relied on the entries in her notes. She recalled a conversation with [Baby I]'s mum about her abdomen. Lucy Letby didn't know whether she'd noticed [Baby I]'s abdomen or whether [Baby I]'s mum had highlighted it to her.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby had noted that [Baby I] appeared generally pale, but she wasn't concerned about [Baby I] being pale as she was often paler in colour. Lucy Letby could not recall how she became aware of [Baby I] vomiting at 4.30 pm or who put out the crash call.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Regarding the incident of 13 October 2015, Lucy Letby did remember this event when [Baby I] was found apnoeic in her cot. She and Nurse Hudson went into the nursery and put the light on in the nursery for something. She explained that the lights weren't switched on in the nursery at night.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby looked over at [Baby I] and noticed that she was paler in colour and her face was pale. Lucy Letby and Nurse Hudson went over to [Baby I] and pulled the covers off her and undid her babygro to check her torso in order to check her colour centrally. [Baby I] was shallow breathing and gasping, the apnoea alarm had not activated as they are programmed to alarm if a baby has not breathed for 20 seconds. If [Baby I] had gasped once every 20 seconds or more, the apnoea alarm would not have gone off.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think in that context the "or more" is probably more than one gasp every 20 seconds rather than a gasp more than every 20 seconds.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She could not recall having treated [Baby I] up to that point of the shift and Lucy Letby started to give Neopuff ventilation and a call for help was made.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: That interview continued the next day on 5 July 2018. The questions moved on to 14 October 2015 and Lucy Letby said she did not remember the shift.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: From the notes, she agreed that she had been [Baby I]'s designated nurse.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In relation to the events of 22 October 2015, Lucy Letby had no recollection of specific events but did remember [Baby I] dying. Lucy Letby had a general recollection of [Baby I] coming and going to and from other hospitals and then coming back to the Countess of Chester, then needing to go back to another hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: There was a feeling on the unit that [Baby I] was being returned to the Countess of Chester too quickly and before she was ready and the transfer process itself was a lot for the baby to undergo and quite stressful for the baby.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: When interviewed again on 11 June 2019, Lucy Letby agreed that she had sent a sympathy card to the [Family of Baby I]. She
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: couldn't go to the funeral and it wasn't often that the nurses would get to know a family as well as they did with the [Family of Baby I]. It was suggested to Lucy Letby that she send a card via one of the other nurses who had gone to the funeral. She had taken a photograph of the card and she -- sorry, she had taken a photograph of the card that she had sent to the [Family of Baby I].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Of the incident on 13 October 2015, Lucy Letby denied injecting air into [Baby I]'s stomach and indicated that she aspirated air from the stomach. During the first collapse, Lucy Letby recalled that [Baby I] was in a cot, not an incubator, she was in the cot space right near the nursery entrance and Lucy Letby agreed that it would have been harder to see whether [Baby I] was pale without the light on.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby could not remember at what point they had put the light on, whether it was before or after they saw [Baby I]. Lucy Letby did not exactly recall the order of events but thought that both she and Ashleigh Hudson were in the nursery together and put the lights on as they went into the room. She thought she and Ashleigh Hudson were at the doorway when she spotted how pale [Baby I] was and that they just put on the lights.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: She could not remember why she'd gone in and turned them on. She could not recall whether [Baby I] was examined prior to putting the lights on.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby wondered whether she, that is Lucy Letby, had seen something in [Baby I]'s colouring that Ashleigh couldn't as she, Lucy Letby, was more experienced. She added that the nursery was never that dark that you wouldn't be able to see the baby at all and there was always a level of light for that reason.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: [Baby I] was often a pale baby, but despite the canopy there was enough light from the corridor to see as [Baby I] was still facing outwards towards the door and there was still light coming in from the main corridor. There was always a degree of natural light that would be on the cot and it was not completely covering [Baby I] so that she was completely out of view.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby could not remember if [Baby I] was wearing a babygro. It was possible she was wearing one with a cardigan. If she was dressed that way, you'd still able to see her face and her hands.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In relation to the incident of 14 October 2015, Lucy Letby denied causing [Baby I] any harm. In relation to the incident of 22 October, she denied causing [Baby I] any harm.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: When interviewed again on 10 November 2020, Lucy Letby denied having administered air to [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby was asked whether she recalled [Baby I]'s feeding tube being out of position and coiled up on 13 October 2015. She did not, but she agreed that it would not be a common event.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: In her texts to [Nurse A] after that shift, she agreed that she'd described [Baby I] as "not good" and that she had asked to care for [Baby I] again the next night for continuity. Lucy Letby explained it was quite common, if on shift, to keep the same baby for continuity of care. She said she would have been a little bit disappointed that there was no continuity, but it did happen and the nurses would not always have the same patients.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lucy Letby was asked why she had searched for [Mother of Baby I] on Facebook and she said she didn't know and she didn't have any recollection of doing it.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That's just a summary so that you have in mind what was said in the interviews. You'll get much more detail and indeed get written records of the relevant parts later on in the case.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Yes.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Yes.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: I was.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: That's right.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think two things. Could you pull the microphone -- sit a little nearer to the microphone and could you please keep your voice up as well. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's a big room, this.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: MOTHER J: So I was in and out of the Countess of Chester Hospital for about 2 weeks prior to having [Baby J], but that was then by emergency section --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: -- at 32 weeks and 2 days.

blocks.text: Were you taken down to the neonatal unit to see [Baby J]?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: I was, but that was much later in the day.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: About 7 o'clock or thereabouts?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Yes, between 7 and 8 pm that evening.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you see [Baby J] when you got there?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: I did, yes. She was in room 1, which is the intensive care room at Chester. She was in an incubator and, yes, she appeared to be doing well, although I was there for about 10 minutes and she produced a little bit of brown bile from the mouth, and then we called one of the nurses over and then they started to investigate what was happening.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Was the outcome of that that [Baby J] was taken over to Alder Hey by ambulance?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Were you told the reason for that at the time?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: We were told that they... Um... That they had concerns about her bowel at that time, yes, because they'd started to do some X-rays and communicate with Alder Hey and share those Xrays. So yes, they had their suspicions that they had identified something on the X-ray.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Was the upshot of it all that you found out that [Baby J] had something called NEC or necrotising enterocolitis?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Yes, that was discussed afterwards, but a perforated bowel was also what was identified.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Did [Baby J] have to spend a period of time at Alder Hey, where she had surgery to deal with that issue?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Yes. She had emergency surgery at Alder Hey the day after she was born on 1 November, around about 9 am in the morning.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did she also have something put in called a Broviac line?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: She did, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So far as [Baby J]'s bowel was concerned, was it in effect cut?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Yes. Yes, they cut the bowel, they removed about 1 centimetre of the bowel and said that that was quite a little amount of the bowel to remove for the concern that they had with the perforation. They then made the decision to give [Baby J] two stomas, which is where the bowel protrudes from the body, and it allows the bowel to rest after the surgery. Then after that, they then reconnect the bowel after a certain period of time.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So the jury haven't really heard anything about this sort of thing before. A stoma is where the bowel in effect exits through the abdomen?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Then there is an entry point as well, so there's an exit and an entry?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Absolutely.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So faeces comes out of the exit?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And was what you had to do eventually is you had to recycle the faeces?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And the purpose of that is to ensure that the second part of the bowel grows at the same rate as the first part?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: That's correct. That's what we were told, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Were you shown how to do that at Alder Hey in Liverpool?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I think you've already told us that [Baby J] was at Alder Hey for about 10 days. She returned, I think, to Chester on 10 November; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Generally, first of all, how much contact did you have with [Baby J] once she'd been returned to Chester?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Very frequent contact with [Baby J]. Mostly in the daytime because there wasn't really the space to stay on the ward.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Were you expressing milk for [Baby J] or was she taking donor milk?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: It was a combination of the two, so I was expressing and we were taking some of the donor milk because I couldn't produce the quantity required.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you fairly quickly establish a routine?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: I did, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Was [Baby J] progressing well?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Absolutely.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And did she in effect cascade down from room 1 to 2 to 3 to 4?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Yes, over a four-week period she progressed to room 4.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So that four-week period essentially coincides with November?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Were there any issues as far as you were concerned?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: There were issues with weight gain. So we expected [Baby J], based on what we'd been told at Alder Hey, to be increasing her weight on a weekly basis and that wasn't happening.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right. Did that concern you?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: It did.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you articulate or communicate your concerns to the staff at Chester?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Frequently.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And how did you feel your concerns were received?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Um... not very seriously. They weren't overly concerned.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: How was the stoma management going?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: We had quite a lot of challenges with the stoma management, but there are two different time periods for that.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. Well, take us through the initial stay at Chester then or the beginning of the -- once you'd returned from Liverpool on 10 November, what were the issues immediately following that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: So in terms of the stoma management?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: So I would say that the faeces that [Baby J] was producing, there was a difference in consistency compared to what we'd seen when we were at Alder Hey for the 11 days, and we'd been informed by the dietician at Alder Hey that if there was a change in consistency then that should be communicated because it was very important to monitor what was going in in
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: terms of feed and then what was coming out in terms of faeces because that's how they measure the -- those were the metrics that they used to analyse what was happening, really.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We didn't see that same approach at Chester, and the management of the stoma -- we spent quite some time managing that ourselves throughout the daytime and it was going quite well for the first 4 weeks, but after that, we started to have some challenges.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What I want to do, if we may, [Mother of Baby J], is just deal with in more detail what happened in November, leading up to 27 November.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Okay.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So, so far as that period of time was concerned, so in absolute date terms the 10th through to 27 November, were there any major problems with the stoma as far as you were concerned?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: No. The only thing I would say is that the bags, the stoma bags, that we were putting on to [Baby J], they should have been lasting between -- well, when we were at Alder Hey they said they'd last for a day, I think between 24 and 48 hours they said they'd last. And at Chester, prior -- for that period, they were probably lasting between 12 and 18 hours, so under what we were expecting.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What I would say is we were -- during that period I was actually trying to breastfeed [Baby J], but because of the stoma bags, whenever we tried to do that, the bag would then leak and cause quite a lot of issues with breastfeeding. But we were at a stage where we could try that because she was doing so well.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Were relations between you, your husband and the staff at Chester good or what?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: I would say that the approach by the staff at Chester was a very different one to the one that we saw at Alder Hey. We felt a little bit like if we asked questions, that they weren't received so well, whereas at Alder Hey it was a very inclusive communication path, whereas I didn't -- [Father of Baby J] and I didn't feel the same about the communication at Chester.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We know, as a matter of record, that at about 7 o'clock in the morning on 27 November, [Baby J] collapsed.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And I just want to deal, if we may, with what happened in the 24 hours or so prior to that collapse.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Yes, sure.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: So the plan was for me to stay overnight for a couple of nights because she was in room 4, we were really excited about getting her home and other than the weight gain issue she was doing extremely well. blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay. So in effect, is this you having a dry run for taking her home --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Yes, absolutely.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: -- with the back-up of the hospital if there were issues?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So can you remember now which the first night was you stayed in the lead-up to the events of the 27th?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: The 25th.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Is that into the 26th?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay. So you'd stayed that night. Did you remain there all day on the 26th as well?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: I think so, yes. I'd made some notes of all the feeds and the cares that I was doing for [Baby J], so I think I was there throughout that day.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What did cares involve?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: So cares involved feeding [Baby J], changing her nappy, and then replacing -- well, attending to the stomas. blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That was quite a lengthy process, so about an hour to just deal with the bag.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: An hour how many times a day?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Three, well, three-hour blocks.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: So... You would literally do the process and then you'd be back at the beginning of it. So at least four -three/four times during the twelve-hour window I was there in the daytime.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay. Did there come a stage on the 26th when you went home?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Prior to...
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Prior to [Baby J]'s collapse.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Yes. Yes, I stayed at home that night.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So you'd stayed the night of the 25th into the 26th, you'd been there all day, you went home on the 26th intending to return on the 27th?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Yes, absolutely. I was there every day from 8 o'clock.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Any particular reason why you picked 8 o'clock as your time of arrival generally speaking?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Because that was after the handover and the staff preferred for parents not to be on the ward when there was a handover of shift.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So you were intending to go at or about 8 o'clock on the morning of the 27th?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: I arrived at 8, so I would leave about 20 to.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. What was the first you heard of an issue involving [Baby J]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: I received a telephone call from a withheld number, basically informing me to get to the hospital very quickly because she'd collapsed.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Let's deal with that. Can you remember roughly what time that call was received?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: I'm trying to think. Maybe about 7.10.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So shortly before you would have left anyway or...?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Mm.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Okay. So you were told that [Baby J] had collapsed; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And in effect get here as quickly as you can?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Absolutely, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And is that what you did?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Were you with your husband?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: I was, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What did you see when you got to the hospital?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: When I got to the hospital, [Baby J] was in a half incubator, so a hot cot, in room 2, which is the high dependency unit, and she was connected back up to a monitor and she looked very floppy. She was very pale, yellowy in colour, and not very responsive.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: How did this event come to you in the sense of what impression did you get as to what had happened?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: We were totally and utterly just shocked because prior to this, she was extremely well, you know, she was coming home, we were preparing for her to come home and look after her in the evening. Everything, other than the weight gain, was fine.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you speak to Dr Gibbs in the aftermath of [Baby J]'s collapse on the 27th?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Yes. [Father of Baby J], my husband, he spoke to Dr Gibbs and had some lengthy conversations with Dr Gibbs. I think I just joined in, you know, a bit later in the conversation.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: I was next to [Baby J] and very stressed by what I was seeing and experiencing.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: She did, yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Yes. Both stomas closed, bowel reattached.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And in due course she went home?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Yes. 5 January, home.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Lovely. Can you just wait there, please?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: MOTHER J: Yes.

blocks.text: I'm seeing if I can help with that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS
